intro.title: Fairness in Data-Driven Algorithmic Loan Approval
intro.p1: When issuing loans, financial institutions are interested in giving loans only to customers who are likely to repay them. If a bank gives a loan to someone who repays it with interest, the bank makes a profit. However, if the loan is not repaid, the bank incurs a loss. Therefore, a bank will aim to maximize its profit.
intro.p2: At the same time, banks are required not to discriminate against different groups of people based on certain protected characteristics (such as gender, origin, religion).
intro.p3: Anyone applying for a loan wants to be evaluated independently of such protected traits or affiliations. In this learning module, you will develop and try out various strategies for distributing loans as "fairly" as possible among different groups of people. To do this, you will first explore the underlying data, develop a decision-making system for loan approval, evaluate it, and then implement various fairness strategies.

twoPopulations.title: Two Population Groups
twoPopulations.subtitle: What do we really find in our data?
twoPopulations.intro1: So far, we have only differentiated the 400 individuals in our dataset by whether they are creditworthy (dark blue) or not (light blue).
twoPopulations.intro2: Our dataset provides even more information. It includes two population groups, each differing in a key characteristic. This characteristic might be gender, ethnicity, or age (such as older versus younger individuals). In our specific example, we classify individuals according to their fictional origin: "Greenfield" and "Pinkville."
twoPopulations.intro3: Each group contains 100 creditworthy and 100 non-creditworthy individuals. Therefore, the probability of being creditworthy is identical in both groups.
twoPopulations.intro4: Despite this, applying the credit score model leads to distinctly different score distributions for the two groups. This difference is evident in the graphics below: For individuals from Pinkville, it is easier to obtain credit due to their on average higher credit scores than for individuals from Greenfield.
twoPopulations.taskA: Discuss why a uniform credit decision based solely on the credit score might be unfair.
twoPopulations.taskB: Consider what it would generally mean for a credit decision to be fair, and formulate a corresponding definition of "fair".

fairThresholds.title: Fair Decision Thresholds!?
fairThresholds.intro: In the following two charts, the data from the two population groups is displayed separately. As a policymaker or societal decision-maker, your role is to define the rules under which banks may operate when granting credit. This includes whether banks are allowed to set different decision thresholds for different groups—or must apply a single, uniform threshold to all applicants.
fairThresholds.tryThresholds: Try different decision thresholds below to work on the following tasks.
fairThresholds.task1: Discuss whether you would choose different decision thresholds for each group or a single threshold for both groups. Decide what you consider to be fair decision thresholds for the two groups that protect individuals from systematic disadvantage while also enabling the bank to operate sustainably.
fairThresholds.task2: Write down the thresholds you have chosen for the two groups.
fairThresholds.task3a: Which statistical measures were important to you when choosing the decision thresholds? Why did you find these measures important?
fairThresholds.task3b: Are your chosen thresholds fair? If yes, why? If not, what would be a fair choice?
fairThresholds.task3c: What is the most important argument for a fair choice of decision thresholds?
fairThresholds.totalProfit: The total profit of the bank is {{profit}}€.

about.title: About This Learning Module
about.articleDescription: This learning activity is based on the following peer-reviewed article, published in Teaching Statistics:
about.articleCitation: Schönbrodt, S., Schneider, S., Podworny, S., & Camminady, T. (2026). A learning activity on fairness in data-driven algorithmic decision-making systems. Teaching Statistics, 48, 33–44.
about.goalText: The activity is designed to develop and analyze various approaches to fairness in data-driven algorithms with highschool students. Students explore different decisions based on credit scores for two groups from a fairness perspective.

measures.title: Statistical Measures
measures.subtitle: Is the decision threshold really well chosen?
measures.intro1: To answer this question and validate the credit approval system, we will use total profit and various statistical measures.
measures.intro2: The decision threshold is used for prediction. If a person has a credit score greater than or equal to the threshold, we predict they will repay the loan. If their score is below the threshold, we predict they will not repay.
measures.intro3: The threshold was initially fixed at 70. For all persons with a score >= 70, we predict repayment. For all others, we predict non-repayment. These predictions can now be compared with the known outcomes.
measures.reminder: Reminder: We are working with data of individuals for whom it is known whether they repaid their loan in the past, and we use this to compare with our predictions.
measures.confusionIntro: The number of correct and incorrect predictions for both groups ("repays" and "does not repay") is shown in the table below. This table is also called a confusion matrix.
measures.task1: How many people receive a loan with a threshold of 70?
measures.task2: How many people receive a loan at threshold 70 who are not creditworthy?
measures.evaluationIntro: There are several statistical measures we can use to evaluate our model:
measures.defAccuracy: Accuracy: Percentage of correct predictions out of all data points.
measures.defPositiveRate: Positive Rate: Percentage of positive predictions (predicts: repays) out of all data points.
measures.defTruePositiveRate: True Positive Rate: Percentage of correct positive predictions out of all actual positive cases (data: repays).
measures.defProfit: Profit: Total profit of the bank (Reminder: the bank earns €300 for each repaid loan and loses €700 for each not repaid loan).
measures.task3: Calculate the values of the four statistical measures using the confusion matrix. Enter your results in the table below.
measures.task4: What percentage of creditworthy individuals actually receive a loan?
measures.task5: What percentage of individuals in the dataset receive a loan?
